title: Deviation Investigation, Lot Disposition and Continuous Improvement

content.overview: When post-harvest conditions deviate from plan, the response should define what happened, which material may be affected, what evidence is available and what disposition is justified. A deviation is not automatically proof of failed product, but it cannot be ignored.

vocabulary.definition: Documented decision about the status or allowed next step for affected material.
Underlying process factor that explains why a deviation occurred.
Corrective and preventive action intended to address a cause and reduce recurrence.

sections.title: Scope the affected material first
sections.body: Use lot genealogy, timestamps and location data to identify which material was exposed to the deviation.

sections.title: Evidence determines consequence
sections.body: Duration, product measurements, sampling and stability knowledge help distinguish a minor excursion from a quality or safety concern.

sections.title: Correct the process as well as the event
sections.body: Repeated deviations should trigger investigation of controls, equipment, staffing or monitoring rather than repeated one-off exceptions.

workedExamples: A short storage-temperature excursion and a prolonged high-moisture drying failure require different evidence and risk review.
If one sensor failed, compare redundant measurements and product data before assuming the entire lot experienced the reported condition.
commonMistakes: Closing a deviation with no affected-lot scope.
Assuming all excursions have identical consequences.
Fixing the immediate symptom without investigating recurrence.
content.practicalApplication: For each deviation record event, timing, affected IDs, available measurements, evidence review, disposition, cause hypothesis and corrective/preventive action.
content.summary: Post-harvest QA turns deviations into documented evidence, scoped decisions and process improvement.
